items.title: Anxiety and Depressive Symptoms in Psoriatic Arthritis: Prevalence and Associations With Sleep, Lifestyle, and Inflammatory Markers.
items.abstract: Anxiety and depressive symptoms are clinically important but frequently under-recognized comorbidities in psoriatic arthritis (PsA). We aimed to estimate the prevalence of anxiety and depressive symptoms in patients with PsA and to explore their associations with demographic, lifestyle, sleep, treatment-related, and inflammatory characteristics. This single-center analytical cross-sectional study included 110 adults receiving treatment for PsA at a specialist rheumatology clinic in Bengaluru, India. Participants completed the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS). Scores of 8-10 and 11-21 on either subscale were classified as borderline and abnormal, respectively; a score of at least 8 was considered screening-positive. Clinical, lifestyle, treatment, baseline erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), and self-reported sleep data were obtained from the study dataset. Associations were tested using two-sided Pearson chi-square tests; exploratory paired sleep responses were assessed with the continuity-corrected McNemar chi-square test. The mean age was 47.4 years (SD 13.7), and 67 participants (60.9%) were women. Twenty-nine participants screened positive for anxiety (26.4%; 95% CI 18.4-35.6), 22 for depression (20.0%; 95% CI 13.0-28.7), and 18 for both (16.4%; 95% CI 10.0-24.6). Baseline sleep disturbance was significantly more frequent among participants with depressive symptoms than among those without depressive symptoms (77.3% vs. 47.7%; Pearson χ²(1)=6.18; p=0.013). Sleep disturbance was also more frequent among participants with anxiety symptoms (69.0% vs 48.1%), although this association did not reach statistical significance (Pearson χ²(1)=3.72; p=0.054). In an exploratory retrospective self-reported comparison, sleep disturbance was reported by 53.6% of participants before treatment and 1.8% after treatment (continuity-corrected McNemar χ²(1)=55.02; p<0.001); this was not a formal prospective follow-up assessment. Approximately one in four participants screened positive for anxiety and one in five for depression. Depressive symptoms were associated with disturbed sleep, whereas baseline ESR and CRP did not distinguish participants with and without psychological symptoms. Routine screening and multidisciplinary assessment may help identify unmet mental health needs in PsA; longitudinal studies with validated disease activity and sleep measures are required.

items.title: Diagnostic Dilemma of Anemia and Oligoarthritis After Tumor Necrosis Factor Inhibitor Therapy in Spondyloarthritis: Flare, Infection, or Paradoxical Reaction?
items.abstract: In patients with axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA), inadequate disease control may necessitate escalation to immunosuppressive therapy. However, subsequent clinical worsening can create a diagnostic dilemma, particularly when disease activity, treatment-related paradoxical reactions, and infection present with overlapping features. We report a 33-year-old man with axSpA receiving targeted synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) therapy who developed peripheral large-joint oligoarthritis. Suspected inadequate disease control led to treatment escalation with a tumor necrosis factor inhibitor (TNFi). He subsequently developed fever, anemia, and worsening arthritis. Infectious workup and synovial fluid analysis were inconclusive. Bone marrow examination showed pure red cell aplasia (PRCA), and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing confirmed a high parvovirus B19 viral load. He improved following treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg). This case highlights the importance of considering parvovirus B19 infection in patients with inflammatory arthritis and unexplained cytopenias, as early diagnosis can prevent unnecessary escalation of immunosuppressive therapy.

items.title: Hypertrophic Discoid Lupus Preceding the Diagnosis of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus With Active Lupus Nephritis: A Case Report.
items.abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a systemic autoimmune disease with heterogeneous cutaneous and visceral manifestations. We report the case of a 26-year-old Japanese woman with SLE who initially presented with a diffuse eruption resembling Kaposi varicelliform eruption and was subsequently found to have severe organ involvement, including active lupus nephritis. The patient had a history of atopic dermatitis, and the eruption was initially treated as Kaposi varicelliform eruption; however, the lesions continued to worsen. The subsequent development of arthralgia, alopecia, and fatigue prompted further investigation, which revealed elevated anti-DNA antibody levels, hypocomplementemia, and newly detected proteinuria. Renal biopsy confirmed active lupus nephritis. Re-evaluation of the cutaneous lesions and the skin biopsy revealed marked hyperkeratosis, epidermal thickening, elongated rete ridges, basal vacuolar degeneration, and lymphocytic infiltration, while direct immunofluorescence demonstrated granular IgA and IgM deposition along dermal vessels. These clinicopathological findings, together with the newly established diagnosis of SLE, supported the diagnosis of hypertrophic lupus, the hypertrophic variant of discoid lupus. Treatment with glucocorticoids, mycophenolate mofetil, voclosporin, and hydroxychloroquine led to remission of the systemic manifestations, including lupus nephritis, with parallel improvement of the skin lesions. This case illustrates that the hypertrophic variant of discoid lupus can mimic other dermatological disorders and delay recognition of systemic disease. Careful assessment of extracutaneous findings is therefore important when evaluating atypical or treatment-refractory skin lesions.

items.title: Therapeutic Strategies Targeting Immune Dysregulation in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus.
items.abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a heterogeneous autoimmune disease driven by loss of immune tolerance, dysregulated nucleic acid sensing and cytokine signaling, abnormal B- and T-cell activation, persistent autoantibody production, and impaired clearance of immune cells and debris. These interconnected abnormalities promote immune-complex formation, complement activation, and multiorgan tissue injury. Recent advances in biologics, small-molecule inhibitors, cellular therapies, and combination regimens reflect an ongoing transition from broad immunosuppression toward mechanism-based treatment. This review summarizes major immunopathogenic mechanisms of SLE and evaluates established and emerging targeted therapeutic strategies according to disease phenotype, trial maturity, efficacy, safety, and principal limitations. The strongest evidence supports type I interferon and B-cell survival blockade, B-cell depletion, and calcineurin-NFAT inhibition, represented by anifrolumab, belimumab, obinutuzumab, and voclosporin. Several Phase 3 programs are evaluating additional TLR, co-stimulatory, FcRn, JAK/TYK2, and B-cell-directed strategies, whereas CD38, BCMA, and cellular therapies remain less mature and require controlled confirmation. Because systemic SLE, lupus nephritis (LN), and cutaneous lupus use distinct populations and outcome measures, efficacy estimates should not be compared directly across phenotypes. Future progress will depend on biomarker-guided patient stratification, rational sequencing of therapy, and careful evaluation of long-term safety, durability, access, and affordability, which may support more personalized treatment in SLE and LN.

items.title: Red Cell Distribution Width and Hematological Patterns in Behçet's Disease.
items.abstract: Objective: Behçet's disease (BD) is a systemic vasculitis characterized by thrombo-inflammation. This cross-sectional study compared inflammatory indices obtained from complete blood counts (CBC), focusing particularly on red blood cell distribution width (RDW), with conventional acute-phase reactants (CRP, ESR). It examined phenotype-specific hematological patterns across clinical manifestations and the cross-sectional relationships of hematological parameters and vascular involvement with treatments. Subjects and Methods: A total of 100 BD patients (ISG criteria) and 42 age- and sex-comparable healthy controls were studied. RDW, MPV, PHR, and CBC-derived indices (NLR, PLR, MLR, SII, SIRI, AISI) were calculated. Disease activity (BDCAF), clinical manifestations (DVT, composite vascular complications, genital ulcer history, arthralgia, pathergy), and treatment regimens were recorded. Between-group comparisons used the Mann-Whitney U test; separation from controls was assessed by ROC analysis with Youden-derived cut-offs. The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure controlled the false discovery rate (FDR) across subgroup comparisons. Results: CRP ( p = 0.299) and ESR ( p = 0.184) did not differ between groups, whereas RDW (median 15.05% [IQR 13.57-16.32] vs. 13.45% [12.90-13.70], p < 0.001) and MPV (8.85 fL [8.38-10.00] vs. 10.05 fL [9.30-10.60], p < 0.001) did. RDW showed the highest observed AUC for separation from controls (AUC 0.77; cut-off > 13.95), followed by MPV (AUC 0.72); CRP (AUC 0.551) and NLR (AUC 0.49) were uninformative. PHR was nominally lower in DVT (median 17.08 [IQR 15.66-18.97] vs. 20.08 [16.54-25.64], p = 0.043) and composite vascular complications (17.16 [15.23-19.28] vs. 20.22 [16.66-26.26], p = 0.024), accompanied by higher hemoglobin ( p = 0.013) and hematocrit ( p = 0.006). RDW was lower in patients with a history of genital ulcers (13.65% [IQR 13.07-14.35] vs. 15.70% [14.17-16.45], p < 0.001). After Benjamini-Hochberg correction, the BD-control differences and the genital ulcer-RDW association remained significant, whereas marginal subgroup associations (DVT-PHR, pathergy-SIRI/AISI; p = 0.02-0.05) did not. Colchicine use was nominally associated with a lower DVT frequency (8.1% vs. 28.6%; OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.05-1.24), an unstable, exploratory finding based on only 14 non-users and substantially confounded by indication. Conclusions: In BD, CBC-derived indices, particularly RDW and MPV, separated BD patients from healthy controls even when conventional acute-phase reactants (CRP and ESR) remained normal, although this reflects separation from health rather than diagnostic accuracy for BD. RDW was lower in patients with a history of genital ulcers, while an exploratory PHR signal in deep vein thrombosis was inconclusive. These readily accessible indices may serve as complementary markers in BD, pending validation in disease-controlled prospective studies.

items.title: Sex-based differences in clinical features associated with the emergence of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus: a nationwide population-based 20-year retrospective study.
items.abstract: There is no single diagnostic test for SLE and disease onset can be insidious, leading to diagnostic delay. We examined clinical events recorded in secondary care prior to SLE diagnosis alongside sex-based differences using a nationwide population databank. We used the Secure Advanced Data Linkage Databank in Wales to construct a national cohort of patients with SLE over a 20-year period (2002-2022). We examined multimorbidities prior to diagnosis and the impact of social deprivation on clinical outcomes using the Welsh Index of Multiple Deprivation. Data were expressed using descriptive analysis and the chi-squared test. A total of 2341 SLE cases (87% female) were identified. Prior utilisation of secondary care services was common (68.2% of cases), most commonly in general medicine (22%), obstetrics and gynaecology (18.6%) and general surgery (13.4%). Essential hypertension (≈15%) and circulatory disorders (≈7%) were both in the top three clinical codes identified in secondary care records prior to SLE diagnosis in males and females. Hypothyroidism (7%) were code-only found in the top five for females. In contrast, idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura was uniquely found in the top five codes in males. The leading recorded cause of death was chest-related infection (33%) and sepsis at 12%. Deprivation analysis showed that SLE was almost three times more common in most-deprived compared with least-deprived areas (15% vs 6%; P  < 0.001). Better understanding of the demographic and clinical factors warranting secondary care services predating a diagnosis of SLE may help avoid diagnostic delay.

items.title: Glucocorticoid prescribing and cardiovascular risk in polymyalgia rheumatica and giant cell arteritis: analysis of routinely collected primary care data from the North of England.
items.abstract: Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) and giant cell arteritis (GCA) are treated with long-term glucocorticoid therapy, which may increase the risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD). Patients with established CVD or with a 10-year CVD risk ≥10%, as estimated by the QRISK tool in primary care, should be offered statins. We aimed to characterise glucocorticoid prescribing and cardiovascular risk in a new primary care PMR/GCA cohort using the Connected Bradford database. We identified patients ≥50 years of age with a new diagnosis of PMR/GCA between 1 January 2000 and 31 December 2023, registered with a general practitioner practice contributing to Connected Bradford for >6 months and with two or more glucocorticoid prescriptions post-diagnosis. Average cumulative prednisolone equivalent dose was calculated in 13-week blocks over a 4-year follow-up period. To characterise CVD risk, the prevalence of diabetes mellitus, atrial fibrillation, heart failure, peripheral arterial disease, hypertension and median QRISK3 scores were estimated on the date of PMR/GCA diagnosis. A total of 4105 patients with PMR and 700 with GCA were identified (66.5% female, mean age 73.6 years). Incidence was 6.27/10 000 person-years for PMR and 1.07/10 000 person-years for GCA. More than one-third of the cohort were still prescribed glucocorticoids 2 years after PMR/GCA diagnosis. At cohort entry, the median QRISK3 score was 29.5%, and 25.3% had pre-existing cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease. There was a considerable burden of CVD, reflected in high QRISK3 scores, alongside frequent prolonged glucocorticoid exposure.

items.title: Factors associated with relapse in ANCA-associated vasculitis: a single-center retrospective cohort study.
items.abstract: Relapse remains common in antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis (AAV). We examined factors associated with relapse after remission. We retrospectively reviewed 130 adults with AAV followed between January 2015 and May 2026, all of whom achieved remission after induction therapy. Demographics, disease subtype, serology, organ involvement, baseline laboratory values, treatments, and relapse were recorded. Relapse was defined as recurrent vasculitic activity after remission requiring escalation/modification of immunosuppressive therapy. Time from remission to first relapse was analyzed using Cox proportional hazards regression, with serious infection modeled as a time-dependent covariate. No imputation was undertaken. Median time from diagnosis to remission was 5.0 months (Q1-Q3: 2.2-7.2) and median observation after remission was 64.8 months (29.9-111.4). Seventy-two patients (55.4%) relapsed and the median time from remission to first relapse was 20.0 months (6.4-50.7). Both multivariable models were fitted on 65 patients with 32 relapse events. In Model 1, serious infection (hazard ratio [HR]: 4.82; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.09-11.10) and rheumatoid factor (RF) positivity (HR: 3.86; 95% CI: 1.68-8.86) were associated with higher relapse hazard. In Model 2, higher total protein was associated with lower relapse hazard (HR: 0.53 per 1 g/dL increase; 95% CI: 0.32-0.88) and RF positivity with higher hazard (HR: 2.66; 95% CI: 1.23-5.74). Low Prognostic Nutritional Index score and lower immunoglobulin G occurred in the relapse group in univariable comparisons only. Relapse affected more than half of the patients who achieved remission. RF positivity showed the most consistent positive association across analyses, although precision varied and CI included the null in one sensitivity model. The serious-infection and total-protein associations were more sensitive to model specification. Given the few events per variable and the missing data, these findings are exploratory and require confirmation.

items.title: Integrated absolute-quantitative gut microbiota profiling and targeted metabolomics reveal microbial and metabolic alterations in children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
items.abstract: Gut microbiota alterations have been implicated in juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), but most previous studies relied on relative abundance profiling and lacked direct metabolite validation. This study aimed to characterise quantitative gut microbiota and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)/organic acid profiles and identify candidate biomarkers in children with JIA. Absolute quantification identified significant differences in α diversity between children with JIA and controls, including Pielou's evenness, Shannon index, and Simpson index, whereas relative quantification detected none. Bray-Curtis dissimilarity, a β-diversity index, also differed significantly between the two groups (PERMANOVA, P < 0.001). At the genus level, Escherichia-Shigella, Flavonifractor, and Methyloversatilis were significantly enriched in JIA patients. Targeted metabolomics revealed divergent faecal and serum metabolic patterns. In faeces, succinate was significantly reduced in JIA patients (fold change = 0.30, adjusted P = 0.005), whereas other faecal metabolites did not reach significance. In serum, acetate, propionate, butyrate, and 2,3-dihydroxy-3-methylbutanoate were significantly elevated in JIA patients, while lactate, malonate, isobutyrate, pentanoate, glutarate, and hexanoate were significantly decreased. Notably, in the full cohort, serum butyrate was markedly elevated in JIA patients compared with controls (median 1543.71 ng/mL, IQR 1237.52-1874.68 vs. 96.98 ng/mL, IQR 78.68-109.65), with a 15.9-fold elevation. In treatment-stratified sensitivity analyses, serum butyrate remained significantly elevated in both drug-naïve patients (n = 15; median 1733.74 ng/mL, IQR 1461.95-2042.70; fold change = 17.9 vs. controls) and drug-exposed patients (n = 34; median 1499.60 ng/mL, IQR 1175.45-1755.05; fold change = 15.5 vs. controls), with no significant difference between the two subgroups. Serum butyrate showed strong discriminatory potential for distinguishing JIA patients from controls, with an optimal cut-off value of 511.94 ng/mL. This study identified gut microbiota and metabolite alterations in children with JIA, and demonstrated that absolute quantification can unmask subtle differences undetectable by relative abundance profiling. The core microbial and metabolic features of JIA are largely disease-intrinsic, yet pharmacotherapy can modulate these features. Serum butyrate shows potential as a biomarker for JIA. This study was registered on April 11, 2023, at the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (registration number ChiCTR2300070403) and at the China National Health Security Information Platform / Medical Research Registration and Filing Information System (registration number MR3323015522).

items.title: Transcriptional analysis of co-stimulatory molecules in ankylosing spondylitis.
items.abstract: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a chronic inflammatory autoimmune disease where T-cell dysregulation plays a pivotal role. A balance of co-stimulatory and co-inhibitory molecules governs the activation of T cells. This study aimed to investigate the mRNA expression profiles of these immune checkpoint signals in AS patients. A cohort of 33 AS patients and 28 healthy controls (HC) from the Taiwanese population was recruited. The mRNA expression levels of five co-stimulatory molecules (CD28, CD40, CD40L, OX40, and OX40L) and one co-inhibitory molecule (TIM-3) were quantified using qRT-PCR. Relative expression was calculated via the 2 -△△ct method, normalized to beta-actin. Significant downregulation of several immune checkpoint molecules was observed in AS patients. Compared with HCs, AS patients exhibited a 2.67-fold reduction in CD28 (p < 0.0001), a 2.37-fold reduction in CD40L (p < 0.0001), a 2.20-fold reduction in TIM-3 (p < 0.0001), and a 1.47-fold reduction in CD40 (p = 0.006). No significant differences were found in the expression of OX40 and OX40L between the two groups. The concurrent downregulation of both activating and inhibitory signals suggests a trend toward coordinated downregulation of the immune checkpoint network in the peripheral blood of AS patients. This phenomenon may represent chronic immune exhaustion or the redistribution of activated immune cells to sites of inflammation. These molecules, particularly CD40L and TIM-3, may represent candidates for further biomarkers that warrant further investigation in large, age- and sex-matched cohorts.

items.title: Gro Health digital app facilitates weight loss and reduces disease activity in psoriatic arthritis.
items.abstract: Obesity is common in psoriatic arthritis (PsA) and is associated with higher disease activity, poorer treatment response, and increased cardiometabolic risk. Digital lifestyle interventions may offer significant support for weight management, but their role in PsA care remains insufficiently explored. To evaluate the impact of a PsA-tailored version of the Gro Health app and digital tier 2 weight management program on patient body weight and disease activity. A secondary objective was to assess patient engagement with this platform as part of a service innovation in routine rheumatology care. This longitudinal observational study recruited 200 adults with PsA and BMI ≥ 25 kg/m² from routine NHS rheumatology clinics at University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire NHS Trust, UK. Of these, 100 patients were offered access to the Gro Health app alongside usual care, and 100 were BMI-matched controls receiving standard care alone. Patients were followed for six months. App engagement, body weight, Composite Psoriatic Disease Activity Index (CPDAI), domain-specific disease activity, and patient-reported outcomes were analyzed. Outcomes were compared between app engagers, non-engagers, and BMI-matched controls. Forty-six patients engaged with the app at least weekly. App engagers achieved significantly greater weight loss compared with non-engagers and controls (- 1.55 kg vs. - 0.18 kg vs. + 1.7 kg; p < 0.001). CPDAI improved in engagers (- 0.58) but worsened in non-engagers and controls (p < 0.001). Improvements were most pronounced in arthritis (p = 0.017) and enthesitis (p = 0.034) domains. Weight loss correlated significantly with improvements in disease activity (ρ = 0.372, p < 0.001). In multivariable analysis, changes in body weight and baseline disease activity remained independent predictors of CPDAI. A multidimensional lifestyle app incorporating tier 2 weight management content, health coaching, and structured digital guidance was associated with modest weight loss and improvements in PsA disease activity, particularly in the arthritis and enthesitis domains. These findings support integrating coached digital weight management strategies into PsA care; however, larger controlled studies are required to confirm efficacy and optimize patient engagement.

items.title: Causal inference framework for personalised b/tsDMARD selection in rheumatoid arthritis: ANSWER cohort validation.
items.abstract: Selecting the optimal biologic or targeted synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (b/tsDMARD) for patients with rheumatoid arthritis remains challenging. We developed and externally validated a causal inference framework combining double machine learning-based causal forests with guideline-derived safety constraints. Using multi-centre registry data from eight Japanese rheumatology facilities (4885 treatment courses), the model was trained on six facilities (n = 2425) and externally validated on two facilities (n = 2460). The framework estimates individualised treatment effects and applies a guideline-based safety rule that excludes Janus kinase inhibitors for patients with multiple cardiovascular risk factors. Patients receiving AI-concordant treatments had higher response rates than those receiving discordant treatments: 33.6% vs 27.2% in crude analysis (absolute risk difference [ARD] = 6.4%, P = 0.002; number needed to treat [NNT] = 16), with consistent effects after propensity score matching (ARD = 5.5%, P = 0.037) and inverse probability of treatment weighting (ARD = 4.3%, P = 0.044). The model identified treatment-effect heterogeneity (group average treatment effects Q4-Q1: Z = 4.64, P < 0.001) and 12 clinically interpretable effect modifiers confirmed by two analytical methods. Benefit was greatest in second-line patients (ARD = 16.0%, NNT = 6.3, P = 0.0002), supporting personalised b/tsDMARD selection.

items.title: Turkish translation, cultural adaptation, and validation of the patient-reported Villalta scale for the diagnosis of postthrombotic syndrome in patients with vascular Behçet disease.
items.abstract: Lower extremity deep vein thrombosis (DVT) constitutes 70% of all vascular findings related to Behçet disease (BD). Postthrombotic syndrome (PTS) is a serious complication of DVT that develops due to chronic venous insufficiency and decreases the patient's quality of life. The physician-reported Villalta scale is a widely used and validated diagnostic tool for diagnosing and evaluating the severity of PTS. However, the necessity of physical examination by a physician burdens the clinician during routine practice. For that reason, a patient-reported Villalta scale was developed and validated. This study aimed to translate the patient-reported Villalta scale into Turkish and validate it. All patients were evaluated using the physician-reported Villalta scale, Clinical-Etiological-Anatomical-Pathophysiological (CEAP) classification, Venous Clinical Severity Score (VCSS), Venous Disability Score (VDS), and patient-reported Villalta scale to diagnose PTS. The VEINES questionnaire and SF-36 were used to evaluate quality of life. Kappa and correlation analysis were performed for validation analysis. One hundred patients with a history of DVT were enrolled in the study, 78 of whom were followed for BD. PTS developed in 52.5% of BD patients with DVT, which was significantly lower compared to non-BD patients (77.3%) (p = 0.038). PTS was detected in 58% (n = 58) of all patients. In kappa compliance analysis of the physician-reported and patient-reported Villalta scales, good agreement was observed (κ = 0.776, p < 0.001). Between the patient-reported and physician-reported Villalta scales, sensitivity was 98%, specificity 76%, positive predictive value 85%, and negative predictive value 97%. This study aimed to validate the Turkish version of the patient-reported Villalta scale to diagnose PTS. The Turkish version of the patient-reported Villalta scale can reliably and validly diagnose PTS. Its application in daily practice may offer useful guidance for clinicians.

items.title: Epicardial adipose tissue thickness and aortic elasticity in seronegative and seropositive rheumatoid arthritis: a comparative evaluation of subclinical cardiometabolic burden.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a systemic inflammatory disease associated with both joint pathology and elevated cardiovascular disease risk. Epicardial adipose tissue thickness (EATT) and aortic elasticity parameters are emerging cardiometabolic markers associated with systemic inflammation and subclinical atherosclerosis. Although the relationship between EATT, aortic elasticity parameters, and RA has been increasingly documented, differences in these parameters between seronegative rheumatoid arthritis and seropositive rheumatoid arthritis remain underexplored. Of the 396 consecutive patients with RA, only those free of established cardiovascular disease and uncontrolled cardiovascular risk factors were included. As a result, 80 patients with RA and 43 healthy controls were included in this study. Aortic elasticity parameters and EATT were measured using M-mode and two-dimensional transthoracic echocardiography. Based on rheumatoid factor and anticitrullinated protein antibody status, patients were classified into seronegative and seropositive subgroups. The mean age of the patients was 53.8 ± 10.5 years. Aortic strain and aortic distensibility were significantly lower, whereas EATT was significantly higher, in patients with RA than in healthy controls. In subgroup analysis, seronegative RA patients had lower aortic strain and aortic distensibility and higher EATT than seropositive RA patients. Moreover, EATT was not significantly correlated with either aortic strain or aortic distensibility in patients with seronegative RA (r = 0.038, p = 0.817; r = 0.187, p = 0.247) or seropositive RA (r = 0.053, p = 0.747; r = 0.073, p = 0.659). Seronegative RA patients exhibited greater EATT and lower aortic strain and aortic distensibility, suggesting increased aortic stiffness and a more adverse subclinical cardiometabolic phenotype.

items.title: Kennedy disease mimicking idiopathic inflammatory myopathy: a 9-year diagnostic delay and case-based review.
items.abstract: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIMs) are frequently considered in patients with proximal weakness and hyperCKemia, but inherited neuromuscular disorders may produce the same initial phenotype. We describe a 56-year-old male technician with 9 years of progressive myalgia, proximal weakness and creatine kinase (CK) elevation who had been treated as having inflammatory myopathy. Although CK decreased during glucocorticoid and leflunomide therapy, muscle strength, walking capacity and bulbar function did not improve in parallel. Reassessment identified long-standing tremor, tongue fasciculations, muscle atrophy and reduced lower-limb reflexes. Myositis serology was negative, thigh magnetic resonance imaging showed diffuse atrophy and fatty replacement without conspicuous active oedema and nerve conduction studies demonstrated reduced or absent sensory nerve action potentials with largely preserved motor conduction velocities. Needle electromyography showed widespread chronic neurogenic abnormalities. Quadriceps biopsy showed advanced chronic, non-specific changes; immunohistochemistry demonstrated only sparse CD68-positive macrophages, no definite CD4-, CD8- or CD20-positive lymphocytic infiltrates, no increased sarcolemmal major histocompatibility complex class I expression and no remarkable C5b-9 deposition. Molecular genetic testing by Sanger sequencing identified 45 CAG repeats in exon 1 of the androgen receptor (AR) gene, confirming Kennedy disease (KD). A focused narrative review identified four relevant reports: three describing KD initially classified as polymyositis and one describing true antisynthetase syndrome coexisting with KD. The present case highlights biochemical-functional discordance as a practical trigger for diagnostic reassessment. In presumed IIM, falling CK without parallel improvement in strength, gait or bulbar function should prompt neurological examination, electrodiagnostic testing and, when clinically indicated, targeted genetic analysis.

items.title: Diet-microbiota Interactions in Rheumatoid Arthritis: Mechanisms and Therapeutic Implications.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a systemic autoimmune disease characterized by chronic inflammation and immunedysregulation. Increasing evidence suggests that the gut microbiota may mediate interactions between environmental factors, particularly diet, and immune responses associated with RA, although causal relationships remain incompletely understood. This review aims to critically evaluate the current evidence on the effects of dietary patterns on gut microbiota composition and function in RA, with particular emphasis on underlying immunometabolic mechanisms, methodological limitations, and clinical relevance. Emerging evidence suggests that the Mediterranean diet and predominantly plant-based dietary patterns are associated with potentially favorable changes in gut microbiota composition, microbial metabolite production, and inflammatory markers. However, evidence that these microbial alterations directly mediate improvements in RA disease activity remains limited. Intermittent fasting may influence microbial circadian rhythms and inflammatory pathways, although much of the mechanistic evidence derives from experimental studies and long-term clinical efficacy remains uncertain. Current evidence does not support routine gluten-free dietary interventions in RA, while probiotic supplementation has shown inconsistent effects on clinical disease activity despite potential improvements in certain inflammatory biomarkers. Diet-microbiota interactions may contribute to immune regulation and inflammatory processes in RA; however, available evidence is limited by methodological heterogeneity, small sample sizes, and potential confounding factors. Although microbiome-guided personalized nutrition represents a promising research direction, its clinical application remains limited by the lack of validated biomarkers and robust intervention studies. Further well-designed, large-scale randomized controlled trials are needed to clarify causal relationships, establish clinically meaningful benefits, and inform evidence-based nutritional recommendations for RA management.

items.title: Melittin: a double-edged sword in rheumatoid arthritis therapy.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic systemic autoimmune disease characterized by persistent synovial inflammation and hyperplasia, which can lead to progressive cartilage and bone damage. Melittin (Mel), the predominant bioactive constituent of bee venom, is an amphipathic, linear cationic peptide exhibiting an α-helical conformation. Mel exhibits anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, and pro-apoptotic effects in synoviocytes and has therefore been investigated as a potential therapeutic agent for RA. Nevertheless, its clinical translation is significantly constrained by inherent biological liabilities, such as potent hemolytic activity, concentration-dependent cytotoxicity, rapid systemic clearance, and a truncated half-life. These properties contribute to both the pharmacological activity and toxicity of melittin, resulting in a narrow therapeutic window. This review summarizes the pharmacological mechanisms of melittin in RA and discusses the major barriers to its clinical translation. The review also evaluates structural modification and drug-delivery strategies that may improve the selectivity, safety, and translational feasibility of melittin.

items.title: Giant-Cell Arteritis.
items.abstract: Giant-cell arteritis is a granulomatous vasculitis of large and medium-sized arteries that occurs almost exclusively in older adults. Suspected giant-cell arteritis warrants urgent diagnostic evaluation and, when ischemic risk is high, immediate treatment before diagnostic confirmation. Although glucocorticoids remain the cornerstone of therapy, treatment is frequently prolonged, associated with substantial toxic effects, and complicated by relapses. Advances in vascular imaging and insights into disease immunopathogenesis have expanded our understanding of disease heterogeneity and enabled the development of targeted therapies, particularly interleukin-6-receptor and Janus kinase inhibitors. Here, we review current concepts in the pathogenesis, clinical presentation, diagnosis, and management of giant-cell arteritis and highlight areas of uncertainty that warrant further investigation.

items.title: FMF-TrackR: real-time digital monitoring of attack triggers in children with Familial Mediterranean Fever.
items.abstract: Familial Mediterranean Fever (FMF) attacks may be influenced by environmental and physiological factors, but evidence on potential triggers is largely retrospective. We aimed to prospectively characterize FMF attacks and their temporal relationship with patient-attributed potential triggers using a real-time digital monitoring platform. Children aged 8-18 years with FMF were prospectively followed from October 2025 to May 2026 using FMF-TrackR, a web-based platform combining weekly assessments with event-based real-time attack reporting. Attack characteristics, potential triggers, and infection onset were recorded contemporaneously. Eighty-five children were followed for 2620 person-weeks; 96.4% of scheduled weekly entries were completed. Forty-nine patients (57.6%) reported 79 attacks, corresponding to 3.02 attacks per 100 person-weeks. Median attack duration was 2.0 days (IQR 2.0-3.0). A potential trigger was reported in 46 attacks (58.2%). Infection was the most frequent trigger (24.1%), followed by psychological stress (17.7%). Infectious symptoms preceded attack onset by a median of 2.0 days (IQR 2.0-3.0). Arthralgia was more frequent in infection-attributed than stress-attributed attacks (57.9% vs. 28.6%, p = 0.048). All six hospital presentations occurred during infection-attributed attacks. Conclusions: Real-time digital monitoring enabled prospective, event-level characterization of FMF attacks and patient-attributed potential triggers with high completion rates. Infection and psychological stress were the most frequently reported triggers. The close temporal relationship between infection onset and FMF attacks highlights the value of contemporaneous monitoring for capturing transient exposures and attack patterns in pediatric FMF.

items.title: METTL1-mediated m7G methylation promoting CD4 + T-cell exhaustion-like phenotype in lupus nephritis.
items.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the association between methyltransferase-like protein 1 (METTL1)-mediated N7-methylguanosine (m7G) methylation and CD4 + T-cell exhaustion-like phenotype in lupus nephritis (LN), using multiomics analyses and bidirectional modulation assays. We collected peripheral blood samples from LN patients and healthy volunteers and renal biopsy specimens from LN patients and peritumoural normal renal tissue controls. Histologically validated Murphy Roths Large/lymphoproliferation (MRL/lpr) mice were used as LN models. Integrated transcriptomic and epitranscriptomic analyses included public database mining, m7G methylated RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing and ribosome profiling sequencing. Functional validation employed tubule-specific methyltransferase-like protein 1 (METTL1) and CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein beta (CEBPB) modulation via adeno-associated viruses in vivo and primary renal cells in vitro. Mechanistic validation included chromatin immunoprecipitation, dual-luciferase reporter assays, and proximity ligation assay. METTL1 expression and global m7G methylation were significantly reduced in renal tubules of LN patients and murine models. Tubular METTL1 deficiency correlated with increased renal CD4 + T-cell exhaustion-like phenotype and renal injury. m7G methylome and ribosome profiling sequencing analyses identified Cebpb as a key downstream candidate associated with METTL1‑mediated m7G changes. Reduced m7G-related enrichment at the Cebpb gene locus was associated with elevated CEBPB steady‑state protein abundance, which directly upregulated the transcription of programmed death‑ligand 1 (PD-L1, encoded by Cd274 ), thereby enhancing PD-L1/programmed death-1 (PD-1) molecular proximity. Conversely, Mettl1 overexpression or Cebpb knockdown attenuated CD4 + T-cell exhaustion-like phenotype and LN progression. Tubular METTL1 deficiency is associated with CD4 + T-cell exhaustion-like phenotype and LN progression, potentially via reduced m7G enrichment at the Cebpb gene locus, increased CEBPB protein, and enhanced PD-L1/PD-1 molecular proximity. Targeting this pathway may mitigate renal injury in LN.

items.title: Silent disabilities in Takayasu arteritis: the overlooked burden of functional decline.
items.abstract: Takayasu arteritis (TAK) is associated with a multidimensional burden that may not be adequately reflected by conventional inflammatory or vascular assessments. Functional performance, fatigue, physical activity, sleep, and quality of life (QoL) may capture complementary aspects of disease impact. To characterize objective functional performance and patient-reported burden in adults with TAK and explore associations of functional performance with disease activity, angiographic extent, treatment exposure, and clinical characteristics. This cross-sectional study included 32 adults with TAK. Functional performance was assessed using the 6-Minute Walk Test (6MWT) and Sit-to-Stand (STS) test; patient-reported outcomes using SF-36, Fatigue Severity Scale, International Physical Activity Questionnaire, and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. Disease activity was assessed using ITAS-2010. The mean age was 47.9 ± 12.9 years, and 87.5% were female. Active disease was present in 65.6% of patients, and 59.4% were receiving corticosteroids. Low physical activity levels were observed in 71.9% of participants. Higher prednisone dose correlated negatively with STS performance (r = -0.404, p = 0.030). BMI was inversely associated with 6MWT distance (r = -0.420, p = 0.021) and positively correlated with fatigue severity (r = 0.515, p = 0.004). Patients with angiographic Type 5 disease exhibited significantly poorer STS performance and shorter 6MWT distances than those with Type 2 a (p = 0.013 and p = 0.041). Active TAK was also associated with fewer STS repetitions (p = 0.042). Objective functional performance was associated with prednisone dose, BMI, angiographic extent, and disease activity. The 6MWT and STS test may complement conventional TAK assessments; longitudinal studies are needed to establish their clinical and prognostic utility.

items.title: Extended MRI versus routine and expert ultrasound in suspected giant cell arteritis: a prospective head-to-head study.
items.abstract: Imaging is central to diagnosing giant cell arteritis (GCA). Ultrasound (US) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are widely used, but prospective head-to-head comparisons are limited. To compare extended MRI with routine US for suspected giant cell arteritis and to assess the influence of US expertise. Ninety-three consecutive patients with suspected GCA underwent US and MRI (median interval 0 days). US assessed the superficial temporal, carotid, subclavian and axillary arteries. MRI additionally evaluated the superficial occipital and vertebral arteries, the thoracic and suprarenal abdominal aorta, and the abdominal aorta. MRI was analyzed (1) restricted to the same vessels as US and (2) including all MRI-assessed vessels (MRI-all). Readers were blinded to clinical data. The reference standard was the final clinical diagnosis after 12 weeks. GCA was confirmed in 45/93 patients. MRI-all vessels showed higher sensitivity than routine US (80% vs. 44%, p < 0.001), with similar specificity (96% vs. 94%). MRI restricted to US-matched vessels also showed higher sensitivity (60% vs. 44%, p = 0.04). Expert US detected 12/15 cases (80%). MRI identified vasculitis in non-US-accessible territories in 9/45 patients (20%). Predictive values reflected the prevalence of the enriched fast-track. Extended MRI was more sensitive than routine US in this fast-track cohort, whereas expert US achieved comparable sensitivity. Ultrasound remains appropriate when expertise is available; MRI is useful for atypical, large-vessel, or inconclusive cases. Question In suspected giant cell arteritis, the diagnostic impact of extended MRI versus routine ultrasound, and the role of ultrasound expertise, remain uncertain. Findings Extended MRI had higher sensitivity than routine ultrasound, but expert ultrasound reached comparable sensitivity; both modalities maintained high overall specificity. Clinical relevance Ultrasound should remain the first line when local expertise is available, while MRI can support atypical, large-vessel, or inconclusive cases.

items.title: Elucidating the molecular interplay between nicotine and ankylosing spondylitis: an integrated systems toxicology study.
items.abstract: This study aims to investigate the potential effects and underlying mechanisms of nicotine on ankylosing spondylitis(AS). Potential targets of nicotine were predicted using the CTD. Gene targets for AS were retrieved from four public databases. Protein-protein interaction network and pathway enrichment analysis were performed. Subsequently, we constructed seven machine learning models using the GSE73754 dataset to identify diagnostic biomarkers. Molecular docking was performed to predict binding affinities and modes, complemented by molecular dynamics simulations for detailed interactions and conformational changes. Lastly, we conducted an in silico knockout experiment using the GSE232131 dataset for validation. After systematic screening of multiple databases, we identified 38 overlapping targets between nicotine and AS. Network analysis refined these to eight hub targets. Enrichment analysis highlighted their significant involvement in inflammatory and immune-related processes, particularly the IL-17 and NF-κB signaling pathway. The logistic regression model exhibited the best predictive performance (AUC 0.905). Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations revealed stable binding complexes, especially with TNF, IL1B and IL10. A virtual knockout experiment revealed TNF as a critical gene within the interaction network. This study provides computational evidence on nicotine's potential impact on AS development. It establishes a foundation for further research on AS preventive and therapeutic strategies. Moreover, the reproducible computational pipeline established can be readily adapted to investigate other environmental triggers in autoimmune diseases and inform the development of evidence-based public health policies related to nicotine exposure.

items.title: Volumetric fat fraction quantification of the sacroiliac joint: changes in axial spondyloarthritis.
items.abstract: To investigate the changes of fat fraction in the sacroiliac joint in axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA), including both the cartilaginous joint and the posterior ligamentous joint (PSIJ), by using a volumetric analyzing method on proton-density fat fraction (PDFF) maps. Patients aged 18-45 years with low back pain that underwent a 3.0 T MRI scan of the sacroiliac joint with additional PDFF maps were retrospectively included. Semi-automatic segmentation of the subcortical region and the PSIJ was performed. Volumetric fat fraction parameters were quantified including histographic analysis. Comparison between axSpA and non-SpA patients was performed. Ninety-three patients including 44 axSpA and 49 non-SpA patients were included. Patients with axSpA had higher mean sacrum PDFF (58.2% vs. 52.5%, p = 0.004). The percentage of bone volume with PDFF ranged from 75% to 100% (i.e. PDFF75100) increased (24.0% vs. 8.9%, p < 0.001), while the percentages of PDFF2550 and PDFF5075 decreased (26.6% vs. 35.6%, p = 0.005, 33.7% vs. 42.0%, p < 0.001). The mean ilium PDFF was not different between groups (p = 0.284), while the percentage of PDFF5075 decreased (39.0% vs. 46.3%, p = 0.033) and the percentage of PDFF75100 increased (20.6% vs.10.6%, p = 0.008). Fat fraction of the PSIJ was not changed in axSpA. The results remained unchanged after correction of age, sex and BMI. By using a volumetric segmentation method, fat fraction of the cartilaginous sacroiliac joint was changed in axSpA while not the PSIJ. Changes of the fat fraction of both the cartilaginous and ligamentous sacroiliac joint was described in detail using a semi-automatic segmentation method.

items.title: Impact of testing method and analyte on the diagnosis of antiphospholipid syndrome: a survey by the association of medical laboratory immunologists.
items.abstract: To evaluate and compare the performance, variation, and agreement of ELISA and non-ELISA methods for detecting anti-cardiolipin (aCL) and anti-beta 2 glycoprotein 1 (aβ 2 GP1) antibodies across clinical laboratories and assess diagnostic standardization. ELISA and non-ELISA methods for IgG, IgM, and IgA aCL and aβ 2 GP1 antibodies were evaluated in patients with antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), APS-like disease, and healthy controls. Agreement (κ and Spearman correlation), sensitivity, specificity, area under the curve (AUC), and relative risk (RR) for APS, thrombotic events (TE), and pregnancy-related morbidity (PRM) were assessed. Correlations were generally stronger within ELISA and within non-ELISA than between ELISA and non-ELISA methods, although substantial inter-assay variability existed within both groups. For APS diagnosis, IgG aCL non-ELISAs demonstrated higher sensitivity than ELISAs (0.73-0.80 vs. 0.50-0.63; p=0.026) with similar specificity (0.96-0.99 vs. 0.94-1.00). AUCs for IgG aCL and IgG aβ 2 GP1 were comparable across individual assays regardless of method (0.83-0.93 and 0.76-0.94, respectively). Non-ELISA IgG aCL assays also showed higher RR estimates for APS (8.3-12.0 vs. 5.7-7.4; p=0.024). However, when aCL and aβ 2 GP1 results were assessed as a complete antibody profile, sensitivity, specificity, AUC, and RR did not differ significantly between ELISA and non-ELISA methods. Generally, the non-ELISAs showed better performance for selected analytes, particularly aCL IgG, while ELISAs demonstrated greater consistency. Although agreement between methods varied for specific antiphospholipid antibodies, overall diagnostic accuracy was comparable when the complete antiphospholipid antibody profile was assessed. Clinicians should consider these factors to ensure accurate and reliable diagnostics.

items.title: Osteopontin and organ damage in systemic lupus erythematosus: A cross-sectional study in Mexican patients.
items.abstract: ObjectiveTo evaluate the relationship between circulating osteopontin (OPN) and irreversible organ damage in Mexican adults with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), and to explore its relationship with disease activity, serological activity, and lupus low disease activity state (LLDAS).MethodsWe conducted a cross-sectional study in consecutive adult patients with SLE from a Mexican tertiary referral centre. Demographic and clinical data were recorded at a single visit. Disease activity was assessed with the SLE Disease Activity Index 2000 (SLEDAI-2K) and irreversible damage with the SLICC/ACR Damage Index (SDI). LLDAS was defined according to published criteria. Plasma OPN concentrations were measured by ELISA. Patients were categorised as having no damage (SDI = 0) or any damage (SDI ≥1).ResultsSeventy-seven patients were included; mean age was 49.8 years (SD 12.9), 75 (97.4%) were women, and median disease duration was 20.0 years (IQR 16.0-25.0). Fifty patients (64.9%) had SDI = 0 and 27 (35.1%) had SDI ≥ 1 (median SDI among damaged patients 1.0, IQR 1.0-2.0). Overall disease activity was low (median SLEDAI-2K 0.0, IQR 0.0-2.0). Median plasma OPN was 15.18 ng/mL (IQR 8.20-52.58). Patients with damage had higher OPN than those without damage (36.23 ng/mL [IQR 11.73-83.62] vs 12.02 ng/mL [IQR 7.77-39.23]; p = 0.017). OPN correlated modestly with SDI total score (ρ = 0.25, p = 0.03). Disease activity was low and showed limited variability (median SLEDAI-2K 0.0, IQR 0.0-2.0), precluding a meaningful assessment of the association between OPN and disease activity.ConclusionsIn this cohort of Mexican adults with long-standing, predominantly quiescent SLE, higher circulating OPN concentrations were observed in patients with irreversible organ damage in unadjusted analyses. The limited variability in disease activity precluded a meaningful assessment of its association with OPN.

items.title: Racial Disparities in Lupus Nephritis: A Nationwide Analysis.
items.abstract: Lupus nephritis (LN) disproportionately affects racial minorities and is associated with significant morbidity and mortality. National-level data on racial disparities in LN remains limited and our study aims to highlight key racial disparities and predictors of inpatient mortality in LN. Cross-sectional observational study. Discharge-level data from US hospitalizations included in National Inpatient Sample database. Adult hospitalizations with a primary/secondary diagnosis of LN were included from National Inpatient Sample (NIS) from 2016 to 2019 using ICD-10 codes and divided into African Americans (AA) or Hispanics versus other races. Not applicable. This was an observational analysis. Several variables, including demographics, outcomes, and health care burden were compared. Multivariate logistic regression was conducted for predictors of mortality. p value of ≤0.05 was considered significant. Among 104, 865 adult LN hospitalizations, 66.3% were AA or Hispanics. Compared with other races, this group were more often females (85.5% vs. 79.9%), younger (38.4 vs. 45.6 y), from lowest-income quartile (45.8% vs. 23.6%), and had Medicaid (30.6% vs. 19.4%). They also had higher rates of acute kidney injury/chronic kidney disease (AKI/CKD) (82.5% vs. 79.1%), ESRD (44.6% vs. 33.9%), and leaving against medical advice (3.0% vs. 1.7%), but lower rates of renal transplant (4.3% vs. 5.2%), transfers to skilled nursing facilities (8.7% vs. 13.3%), and mortality (1.7% vs. 2.6%). Significant mortality predictors included: age, Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), Medicaid, small bed size, sepsis, pulmonary embolism/deep vein thrombosis (PE/DVT), and CKD. (All p≤0.05 unless specified). Review of medical data from an administrative database involved reliance on diagnostic coding, limited detailed clinical information, and residual confounding. African Americans and Hispanics represented two-thirds of LN hospitalizations and had distinct demographic profiles, reflecting greater socioeconomic disadvantage and renal disease burden. Mortality was influenced by age, comorbidity burden, Medicaid status, hospital size, sepsis, PE/DVT, and CKD highlighting key factors influencing potential disparities.

items.title: Glucocorticoid discontinuation and flare risk in remitted systemic lupus erythematosus: a propensity score-matched cohort study.
items.abstract: To assess flare risk during remission in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) patients comparing low-dose glucocorticoid (GC) maintenance and its discontinuation. Prospective data of SLE patients were retrospectively evaluated. Remission was defined as clinical-SLEDAI-2K=0 on prednisone (PDN) dose ≤5 mg/day and stable background therapy, flares as any increase in clinical-SLEDAI-2K>0 or escalation in SLE medications. Patients withdrawing GC (off-GC) during remission were compared with patients on PDN≤5 mg/day (on-GC) through propensity score matching (PSM). Time-varying exposure Cox regression and Simon-Makuch curve assessed flare predictors and flare-free remission. Among 541 patients, 480 achieved remission and 358 (74.6%) discontinued GC. 86 flares occurred: 48 in off-GC (2.07 flare/100 patients-year) and 38 in on-GC patients (3.44 flares/100 patients-year, 1.66 on/off-GC ratio). Flare-free survival (p = 0.189) and flare hazard (HR 0.727, 95%CI 0.450-1.172, p = 0.19) were similar in off and on-GC patients; results were confirmed after adjustment for baseline covariates (HR 0.673, 0.401-1.128, p = 0.1326). Skin rash (HR 1.997, 1.061-3.76, p = 0.032), arthritis/myositis (HR 2.827, 1.103-7.246, p = 0.03), leukopenia (HR 1.852, 1.004-3.415, p = 0.048), and vasculitis (HR 3.521, 1.691-7.33, p < 0.001) were associated with flare in off-GC patients. In PSM cohort (314 off-GC and 114 on-GC patients), no significant increase in flare rate was found during remission after GC discontinuation (HR 0.767, 0.386-1.524, p = 0.45). Flare occurrence in off-GC patients was not associated with damage accrual (IRR 1.598, 95%CI 0.746-3.424, p = 0.227). Glucocorticoid withdrawal was not associated with an increased flare hazard in SLE patients compared to low-dose maintenance.

items.title: Association of self-reported long-term or recurrent childhood antibiotic use and axial spondyloarthritis among HLA-B27-positive individuals.
items.abstract: To examine whether self-reported long-term or recurrent antibiotic use during childhood or adolescence is associated with axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) diagnosis among HLA-B27-positive individuals. We studied HLA-B27-positive adults of White European ancestry in UK Biobank who reported long-term/recurrent (≥3 courses/year) antibiotics during childhood/adolescence. AxSpA was ascertained from linked hospital, death and primary care records. Logistic regression estimated age- and sex-adjusted odds ratios (ORs). We assessed robustness using sensitivity analyses, positive and negative control outcomes (anterior uveitis and rheumatoid arthritis), quantitative bias analysis for differential recall, and construct validation in linked primary care data. Among 10,528 HLA-B27-positive participants, 206 had axSpA and 1,481 reported long-term/recurrent childhood/adolescent antibiotic use. Childhood exposure was associated with two-fold higher odds of axSpA diagnosis than none (OR 2.02, 95% CI 1.42-2.89; p < 0.001), with consistent estimates across sensitivity analyses. Associations with control-outcome were OR 1.80 (1.07-3.03) for anterior uveitis and 1.29 (0.87-1.91) for rheumatoid arthritis. In a separate construct-validation cohort of 57,627 participants with linked primary care data, self-reported childhood exposure identified a persistent high-antibiotic-use phenotype, with higher later-life prescription rates (adjusted incidence rate ratio 1.75, 95% CI 1.42-2.14) and exposure duration (2.14, 1.59-2.88); higher prescribing persisted after accounting for infection episodes. Under differential-recall assumptions, the median bias-adjusted OR was 1.72 (95% simulation interval 1.08-2.72) but adverse stress test attenuated OR to 1.42 (0.69-2.61). Self-reported early-life long-term/recurrent antibiotic use was associated with two-fold higher odds of axSpA among HLA-B27-positive individuals. Future research should examine antibiotic versus infection effects and potential microbiome mediation.

items.title: Isolated pulmonary Capillaritis presenting as massive Hemoptysis: a rare pulmonary manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis in a young female.
items.abstract: Pulmonary manifestations of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) most commonly include interstitial lung disease, pleural effusions, and rheumatoid nodules. Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH) due to isolated pulmonary capillaritis is an exceptionally rare and potentially fatal presentation, particularly in young adults with high serology-positive articular disease. A 27-year-old female with a known history of rheumatoid arthritis, hyperlipidemia, carpal tunnel syndrome and hyperthyroidism presented to the emergency department with acute chest pain, progressive shortness of breath, and massive hemoptysis. She developed hypoxemic respiratory failure requiring intensive care unit admission. On presentation, her blood pressure was 100/70 mmHg, heart rate 111 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 19 breaths per minute. Chest computed tomography (CT) revealed bilateral diffuse ground-glass opacities consistent with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH). Bronchoscopy with sequential bronchoalveolar lavage confirmed ongoing alveolar hemorrhage. Infectious studies were negative. Serologic evaluation for systemic vasculitis, including ANCA-associated vasculitis and anti-glomerular basement membrane disease, was unremarkable. Autoimmune testing demonstrated markedly elevated rheumatoid factor, ESR, CRP and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies. Given persistent diagnostic uncertainty, a surgical lung biopsy was performed and demonstrated isolated pulmonary capillaritis without granulomatous inflammation or immune complex deposition. A diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis-associated pulmonary capillaritis presenting as DAH was established. The patient was treated with pulse-dose intravenous corticosteroids followed by additional immunosuppressive therapy of rituxumab, resulting in rapid clinical and radiographic improvement. A repeat chest CT performed one month after initiation of corticosteroid and rituxumab therapy showed significant resolution of the previously noted ground-glass opacities. Isolated pulmonary capillaritis due to rheumatoid arthritis should be considered in cases of unexplained massive hemoptysis. Although rare, rheumatoid arthritis (RA) can present with life-threatening pulmonary hemorrhage, highlighting the need for early multidisciplinary evaluation and prompt initiation of immunosuppressive therapy.

items.title: [Expert consensus on blood pressure and vascular assessment and multidisciplinary management of adult Takayasu arteritis (2026 edition)].
items.abstract: Takayasu arteritis-related hypertension (TARH) is common and often refractory, leading to severe target organ damage involving the heart, brain, kidneys, and major vessels, which significantly impacts patient prognosis and is a major cause of death in patients with Takayasu arteritis. However, there is currently no unified consensus on systematic evaluation and standardized management in clinical practice. To address this, the Zhongshan Hospital of Fudan University took the lead, in collaboration with the Rheumatology Branch of Chinese Women's Medical Association, Rheumatism Committee of Chinese Association of Integrative Medicine, Rheumatology Branch of Shanghai Medical Association, and multidisciplinary experts from across China. On the basis of the "Chinese multidisciplinary recommendations on the diagnosis and treatment of Takayasu's arteritis-related hypertension" published in 2021, this consensus has been updated to address key issues in TARH, including epidemiology, definition, early identification and comprehensive assessment of high-risk populations, antihypertensive drug therapy, and revascularization, with 16 core clinical questions identified. Through evidence retrieval and multiple rounds of discussion and voting, 28 recommendations have been formulated. This consensus aims to standardize clinical decision-making in TARH, improve blood pressure control rates, reduce target organ damage, and improve the long-term prognosis of Chinese TARH patients. 大动脉炎相关高血压（TARH）常见且难治，所致心、脑、肾及大血管等靶器官损害严重影响患者预后，是大动脉炎患者死亡的重要原因之一，但临床缺乏系统评估与规范化治疗的统一共识。为此，由复旦大学附属中山医院牵头，联合中国女医师协会风湿免疫女医师分会、中国中西医结合学会风湿类疾病专委会、上海市医学会风湿病学分会及国内相关学科专家，在2021年发布的《中国大动脉炎相关高血压诊治多学科专家共识》基础上，围绕TARH的流行病学、定义、高危人群的早期识别与全面评估、降压药物治疗、血运重建等关键问题进行更新，系统梳理并提出了16个核心临床问题，经证据检索与多轮讨论投票，形成28条推荐意见，旨在规范TARH临床决策，提高血压达标率，减少靶器官损害，改善我国患者远期预后。.

items.title: From Disease Susceptibility to Prognosis in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus-Associated Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension: A Systematic Review.
items.abstract: Background: Systemic lupus erythematosus-associated pulmonary arterial hypertension (SLE-PAH) is a severe complication requiring early recognition and risk stratification. However, factors associated with prevalent disease, non-invasive detection, incident PAH, and prognosis after diagnosis are frequently conflated. Methods: PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library were initially searched through 23 September 2026, and searches of all four databases were updated on 1 November 2026. Observational evidence was evaluated using a structured clinical-pathway framework and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, and findings were synthesized narratively because of clinical and methodological heterogeneity and potentially overlapping cohorts. Results: Thirty-five studies were included in the qualitative synthesis. Serositis, interstitial lung disease, pericardial effusion, anti-U1 RNP and anti-Ro/SSA antibodies, reduced diffusing capacity, and microvascular abnormalities were mainly associated with prevalent or concomitant disease. Non-invasive detection was supported by a multimodal approach incorporating symptoms, biomarkers, pulmonary function, and echocardiography, with right heart catheterization required for PAH confirmation. Evidence on incident, catheterization-confirmed PAH prediction was limited. After diagnosis, functional class, exercise capacity, pulmonary vascular load, right-heart function, and serial risk status were recurrent prognostic indicators. Conclusions: Evidence is more extensive for prognosis after established SLE-PAH than for incident prediction, highlighting the need for externally validated SLE-specific screening and risk-stratification tools.

items.title: Redox Control of Mesenchymal Stromal Cell-Mediated Immunoregulation in Rheumatoid Arthritis: From Licensing to Stromal Inflammaging.
items.abstract: Mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) are dynamic regulators of the immune response whose immunomodulatory functions are influenced by inflammatory cues. In rheumatoid arthritis (RA), acute inflammatory signals enhance MSC function through licensing, whereas chronic exposure to the inflammatory microenvironment promotes mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, senescence, and loss of immunoregulatory capacity. In parallel, fibroblast-like synoviocytes (FLS) undergo metabolic and mitochondrial reprogramming that promote inflammatory activation, apoptosis resistance, and tissue-destructive behavior. This structured narrative review examined the literature on MSC licensing and T-cell regulation in rheumatoid arthritis. A comprehensive literature search of ScienceDirect, Web of Science, and PubMed was conducted in September and November 2026 to identify relevant studies published between 1990 to 2026. Search terms included combinations of "mesenchymal stem/stromal cells", "T-cells", "rheumatoid arthritis", "RA", "priming/licensing", "immunomodulation", "mitochondrial dysfunction", "metabolic reprogramming", and "synovial environment". Original research articles and reviews were included. Of 273 initially identified articles, 182 remained after duplicate removal, and 125 were included in the final analysis. Studies were considered eligible if they addressed relevant information on MSC licensing, MSC immunomodulation, mitochondrial metabolism, or stromal-immune interactions in RA. Evidence from human-derived cells and experimental arthritis models was considered. Mechanistic studies in non-RA models were included where they provided relevant insights into the underlying mechanisms of MSC licensing and T-cell regulation. Studies were excluded if they lacked sufficient relevance to RA, did not provide original experimental data, or contained insufficient mechanistic information. Screening was performed by S.S. and J.D. and evaluation was conducted separately before comparison. Findings from human RA samples and experimental models suggest that inflammatory licensing can transiently enhance MSC-mediated immunosuppression through metabolic adaptation, whereas prolonged inflammation is associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, redox imbalance, and senescence. These changes may reduce the capacity of MSCs to suppress pathogenic T-cell responses. In parallel, RA-FLS exhibit altered glycolytic and lipid metabolism, mitochondrial dysfunction, and increased inflammatory and invasive behavior. These findings suggest that metabolic dysregulation may reinforce stromal-immune interactions that propagate synovitis; however, the precise mechanism has not been elucidated in RA patient-derived MSCs. This review provides an integrated framework linking inflammatory licensing, metabolic flexibility, mitochondrial homeostasis, and stromal-immune interactions to understand MSC immunoregulatory function in RA and the contribution of FLS to RA pathogenesis. Here, we highlighted processes contributing to persistent synovial inflammation and identified potential targets for therapeutic intervention. Strategies to preserve metabolic flexibility and mitochondrial homeostasis warrant further investigation, but mechanistic confirmation in human RA models and clinical studies is needed before potential therapies can be developed.

items.title: Impact of cardiovascular risk factors and atherosclerosis-related diseases on the OMERACT giant cell arteritis ultrasound score.
items.abstract: To evaluate the impact of cardiovascular risk (CVR) factors and atherosclerosis-related diseases on the OMERACT Giant Cell Arteritis Ultrasound Score (OGUS) in patients with suspected giant cell arteritis (GCA). This retrospective monocentric study included all patients undergoing temporal and axillary artery ultrasonography for suspected GCA between January 2022 and May 2025 in a fast-track clinic. CVR factors (systemic hypertension, diabetes, hypercholesterolaemia, smoking) and atherosclerosis-related diseases (coronary artery disease, peripheral arterial disease, ischaemic stroke, chronic kidney disease) were recorded. Intima-media thickness was measured and OGUS calculated. Associations between OGUS and cardiovascular variables were assessed in the whole population and in the GCA subgroup, using univariate and multivariate linear regression analyses. Among 152 patients, 72 met the 2022 ACR/EULAR classification criteria for GCA. OGUS and cranial OGUS were significantly higher in GCA than in non-GCA patients ( P  < 0.001). In the whole population, OGUS was higher in those with systemic hypertension and increased with age. In GCA patients, OGUS was higher in males and in those with hypercholesterolaemia, and was positively correlated with age. Multivariate analysis confirmed age as independent determinants of OGUS in this subgroup. OGUS was not associated with ischaemic complications of GCA, including ophthalmic events and inflammatory strokes. In the univariate analysis in GCA, OGUS was higher in male, with hypercholesterolemia and increased with age. In the multivariate analysis, age was still associated with higher OGUS. CVR factors should be considered when interpreting OGUS at diagnosis and during follow-up in clinical trials.

items.title: Metabolomics in ankylosing spondylitis: insights into pathogenesis and biomarker discovery.
items.abstract: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a persistent inflammatory condition whose underlying mechanisms are not yet fully understood, though they seem to involve a complex interplay of genetic and environmental influences. Increasing evidence has highlighted a significant link between metabolomics research and the development of AS. This review comprehensively examines the key metabolomics studies related to AS, exploring how such research can illuminate the disease's pathogenesis and aid in the identification of potential biomarkers.Additionally, it discusses the potential implications of these findings for improving diagnostic and therapeutic strategies.

items.title: Association Between Anti-Ro52 Antibody Concentration and Documented Depression in Patients with Sjögren's Disease: A Retrospective Observational Study.
items.abstract: Background/Objectives : Depression is a clinically relevant neuropsychiatric manifestation of Sjögren's disease, although the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Autoimmune and neuroinflammatory processes, including the potential role of autoantibodies, may contribute to its development. This study aimed to investigate the association between anti-Ro antibodies, with particular emphasis on anti-Ro52, and the presence of depression in patients with Sjögren's disease and to explore whether quantitative anti-Ro52 antibody levels may provide patient-level information relevant to a more personalized assessment of neuropsychiatric manifestations. Methods : This retrospective, observational, cross-sectional study included 141 adult patients with Sjögren's disease treated at the University Hospital of Split between 2020 and 2023. Depression was defined as a documented diagnosis supported by psychiatric evaluation. The association between anti-Ro52 antibody concentration and depression was assessed using Firth's penalized logistic regression, adjusted for age and sex, with correction for multiple testing using the false discovery rate procedure. A sensitivity analysis was performed after restricting the analysis to patients with primary Sjögren's disease. Results : Depression was documented in 16/141 patients (11.3%). Anti-Ro52 concentrations were available for 111 patients, including 13 with depression. Higher anti-Ro52 concentrations were significantly associated with lower odds of depression. A one-standard-deviation increase in anti-Ro52 concentration was associated with 70% lower odds of depression (OR 0.30; 95% CI 0.12-0.61; p < 0.001). The association remained significant after multiple-testing correction (overall FDR-adjusted p = 0.046). The inverse association remained significant in the sensitivity analysis restricted to patients with primary Sjögren's disease (OR per 1-SD increase = 0.38; 95% CI 0.14-0.82; p = 0.013). Conclusions : Higher anti-Ro52 antibody concentrations were associated with lower odds of documented depression in patients with Sjögren's disease after adjustment for age and sex. These findings suggest that quantitative serological profiling may provide patient-level information relevant to a more personalized assessment of neuropsychiatric manifestations. However, prospective studies using standardized depression assessments are required to determine the clinical relevance and potential utility of anti-Ro52 levels in individualized patients.

items.title: ISG15+ CD4+ T cells are enriched in anti-MDA5 dermatomyositis and promote IL-1β production via LFA-1.
items.abstract: Anti-MDA5 dermatomyositis (DM) is characterised by high risk of rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease (ILD) and a prominent type I interferon (IFN) signature. We aimed to delineate IFN-stimulated CD4+ T-cell subsets in anti-MDA5 DM and elucidate their pathogenic roles. Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed on skeletal muscle biopsies from anti-MDA5 DM (n=3), anti-synthetase syndrome (n=3) and healthy controls (n=3). CD4+ T-cell ISG15 expression was quantified by flow cytometry in peripheral blood from dermatomyositis cohorts (n=86), other inflammatory myopathies (n=35) and healthy controls (n=39), including paired pre-/post-treatment samples (n=10). Serum CCL19 was determined by ELISA. Mechanistic insights were gained through in vitro stimulation of CD4+ T cells with IFNβ or recombinant ISG15, and functional validation using LFA-1 blockade. Muscle single-cell profiling unveiled a unique ISG15+CD4+ T-cell cluster exclusively detected in anti-MDA5 DM, transcriptionally enriched for type I IFN and antiviral responses. In peripheral blood, CD4+ T-cell ISG15 geometric mean fluorescence intensity (gMFI) was significantly elevated across dermatomyositis cohorts compared with healthy controls and other myositis subtypes, peaking in anti-MDA5 DM. Notably, ISG15 gMFI diminished following immunosuppressive therapy and correlated with systemic inflammatory markers as well as biomarkers associated with ILD presence (ferritin and KL-6). Transcriptionally, this cluster displayed CCR7 enrichment; correspondingly, circulating CCR7+ CD4+ T cells and serum CCL19 concentrations were significantly increased in anti-MDA5 DM. Functionally, IFNβ stimulation recapitulated the ISG15, phenotype and triggered its secretion. Extracellular ISG15 potentiated IL-1β transcription and release from CD4+ T cells via LFA-1, as shown by blockade inhibition. ISG15+ CD4+ T cells constitute a treatment-responsive, IFN-driven pathogenic axis in anti-MDA5 DM, amplifying inflammation via ISG15-LFA-1-mediated IL-1β production. These findings identify a novel therapeutic target in this high-risk ILD complication.

items.title: Severe Progressive Multifocal Axonal Neuropathy After a Prolonged Fibrotic Interstitial Lung Disease Phase in MPO-ANCA-Associated Vasculitis: A Case Report.
items.abstract: Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) is an antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated small-vessel vasculitis that may affect multiple organs. Interstitial lung disease (ILD), particularly with a usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern, may precede systemic vasculitis and delay diagnosis. We report a patient with initially undifferentiated fibrotic ILD identified in 2023, with radiological suspicion of UIP/IPF. The initial immunological evaluation in December 2023 was inconclusive: ANCA testing by indirect immunofluorescence was non-diagnostic, while antigen-specific MPO-ANCA and PR3-ANCA assays were negative. Over the following two years, the patient developed recurrent fever, progressive respiratory symptoms, systemic inflammation, anaemia, renal impairment, and severe bilateral lower limb weakness leading to loss of ambulation. Electroneurography demonstrated a severe, predominantly axonal sensorimotor neuropathy with multifocal involvement, while sural nerve biopsy revealed vascular inflammatory changes, raising the possibility of vasculitic neuropathy, although chronic thrombotic microangiopathy remained a possible coexisting process. In October 2025, markedly elevated MPO-ANCA levels were detected during evaluation of progressive multisystem disease. Whether this change reflected seroconversion during disease evolution or differences related to earlier testing cannot be determined retrospectively. The diagnosis of MPA was supported by the combination of markedly elevated myeloperoxidase (MPO)-ANCA levels, fibrotic ILD, renal dysfunction, systemic inflammation, severe multifocal neuropathy, and the nerve-biopsy findings. Treatment with high-dose corticosteroids, rituximab, intravenous immunoglobulin, and rehabilitation was followed by partial neurological recovery, although significant lower limb deficits persisted. This case illustrates the diagnostic challenges posed by severe MPO-ANCA-associated vasculitis following a prolonged fibrotic ILD phase. However, the available evidence does not establish whether the initial pulmonary fibrosis was an early manifestation of vasculitis or a coexisting fibrotic lung disease. The case also demonstrates that meaningful functional improvement may occur despite severe electrophysiological abnormalities.
